a.onclick: openModal( this, "Non-functional mRNA", ["41612912"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41612912"], ["During IVT and downstream handling, mRNA can be nicked or partially degraded by RNases, heat, shear, or chemical stress, generating shorter fragments that lack a full ORF, proper cap, or poly(A) tail. Manufacturers therefore use stringent QC (fragment analysis, LC–MS, cap and tail assays) and purification steps to minimize these species, but they can never be completely eliminated. Once such fragments enter cells, they are quickly recognized as poor translation substrates and removed by the same pathways that clear endogenous defective mRNA. These non‑functional RNAs mainly reduce the effective dose of productive mRNA and can contribute modestly to innate immune sensing (if they form dsRNA)."])

openModal( this, "dsRNA (duplex or harpin)", ["11607032"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11607032"], ["Unlike PKR, RIG-I, and MDA5, which float freely in the cell's fluid cytoplasm, TLR3 is an endosomal membrane receptor. When IVT mRNA is spilled in the endosomal lumen before escaping in the cytoplasm, dsRNA fragments - that are at least 40-50 base pairs long - bind two TLR-3 molecules that act as homodimers. Then, IRF3/IRF7 and and NF-kB drive the expression of, respectively, Type I Interferons (specifcally IFN-β) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-12, and TNF-α)."])

openModal( this, "U-rich unmodified ssRNA", ["36351374"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36351374"], ["Non-modified IVT mRNA is intrinsically immunostimulatory because cells recognize it as a “viral” RNA through multiple innate sensors, especially when it carries unmodified uridines. Endosomal toll-like receptors TLR-7 and TLR-8 bind single‑stranded uridine‑rich RNA and activate NF‑κB, producing pro-inflammatory cytokines, and IRF7, producing type I IFN."])

openModal( this, "NF‑κB, IRF3, and IRF7", ["36351374, 38528828"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36351374","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38528828"], ["NF‑κB, IRF3, and IRF7 are transcription factors that sit at the core of the innate response to therapeutic mRNA, controlling inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons once RNA‑sensing pathways are engaged. Therapeutic mRNA (especially unmodified or dsRNA‑contaminated IVT mRNA) is sensed as foreign RNA by pattern‑recognition receptors (PRRs), which converge on these three transcription factors.","For modern RNA vaccines (e.g., m1Ψ‑modified, Cap1‑capped), nucleoside modification and purification reduce activation of these pathways, although not completely abolishing it. Residual NF‑κB and IRF3/7 activity provides useful self‑adjuvant effects (DC maturation, costimulatory molecule upregulation, chemokine production) but excessive activation would suppress translation and increase reactogenicity, so sequence, chemistry, and LNP design all aim to keep their activation transient and tuned rather than maximal."])

openModal( this, "NF‑κB, IRF3, and IRF7", ["36351374, 38528828"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36351374","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38528828"], ["NF‑κB, IRF3, and IRF7 are transcription factors that sit at the core of the innate response to therapeutic mRNA, controlling inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons once RNA‑sensing pathways are engaged. Therapeutic mRNA (especially unmodified or dsRNA‑contaminated IVT mRNA) is sensed as foreign RNA by pattern‑recognition receptors (PRRs), which converge on these three transcription factors.","For modern RNA vaccines (e.g., m1Ψ‑modified, Cap1‑capped), nucleoside modification and purification reduce activation of these pathways, although not completely abolishing it. Residual NF‑κB and IRF3/7 activity provides useful self‑adjuvant effects (DC maturation, costimulatory molecule upregulation, chemokine production) but excessive activation would suppress translation and increase reactogenicity, so sequence, chemistry, and LNP design all aim to keep their activation transient and tuned rather than maximal."])

openModal( this, "NF‑κB, IRF3, and IRF7", ["36351374, 38528828"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36351374","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38528828"], ["NF‑κB, IRF3, and IRF7 are transcription factors that sit at the core of the innate response to therapeutic mRNA, controlling inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons once RNA‑sensing pathways are engaged. Therapeutic mRNA (especially unmodified or dsRNA‑contaminated IVT mRNA) is sensed as foreign RNA by pattern‑recognition receptors (PRRs), which converge on these three transcription factors.","For modern RNA vaccines (e.g., m1Ψ‑modified, Cap1‑capped), nucleoside modification and purification reduce activation of these pathways, although not completely abolishing it. Residual NF‑κB and IRF3/7 activity provides useful self‑adjuvant effects (DC maturation, costimulatory molecule upregulation, chemokine production) but excessive activation would suppress translation and increase reactogenicity, so sequence, chemistry, and LNP design all aim to keep their activation transient and tuned rather than maximal."])

openModal( this, "Type I interferons", ["37834268"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37834268"], ["Once IRF3/IRF7 signalling has driven their transcription and the cell secretes them, type I interferons (IFN-α/β) act back on the same cell and its neighbours by binding the type I IFN receptor (IFNAR), which engages the JAK–STAT cascade and switches on hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). The interferon itself does not degrade the mRNA, instead, it induces a set of latent sentinel effectors, mainly PKR and OAS/RNase L. What then activates these effectors is the mRNA itself, so the same molecule that ignited the interferon cascade also prepares and then engages its effectors."])

openModal( this, "m¹Ψ, Ψ, m⁵C modified ssRNA", ["36351374"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36351374"], ["To tame this immunogenic response, current mRNA therapeutics rely heavily on nucleoside base modifications that reduce innate sensing while preserving or enhancing translation. Replacing uridine with pseudouridine (Ψ) or, more commonly now, N1‑methylpseudouridine (m1Ψ) attenuates activation of TLR-7/8, lowers type I IFN induction, and increases protein yield in vitro and in vivo. Additional or alternative modifications include 5‑methylcytidine (m5C) and N6‑methyladenosine (m6A), which can further tune RNA structure, stability, and recognition by RNA‑binding proteins, and emerging synthetic bases such as base Z (2‑aminoadenine) have also been shown to reduce immunogenicity and improve translation in experimental systems."])

openModal( this, "If premature STOP (NMD)", ["22664987"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664987"], ["Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) targets mRNAs in which translation terminates too early, at a premature termination codon (PTC), and is triggered when a stop codon is perceived as abnormal based on features downstream of it. UPF factors associate with the terminating ribosome at the PTC, interpret the downstream context as “premature,” and then recruit general decay machinery (decapping, deadenylation and sometimes endonucleolytic cleavage) to rapidly destroy the mRNA while also targeting the truncated peptide and helping recycle the ribosome."])

openModal( this, "If NO STOP codon (NSD)", ["22664987"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664987"], ["Non-stop decay (NSD) is engaged when ribosomes reach the 3′ end of an mRNA without encountering a stop codon, for example on truncated transcripts or on RNAs whose coding sequence runs directly into the poly(A) tail. In the latter case, decoding of the poly(A) tail produces poly-lysine stretches that stall the ribosome in the exit tunnel long before it reaches the physical end of the RNA, creating a stable arrested complex that defines NSD substrates. These fragments promote endonucleolytic cleavage upstream of the stall, and ensure that both mRNA fragments and the aberrant nascent chain are degraded while ribosomal subunits are recycled."])

openModal( this, "If ribosome stalling (NGD)", ["22664987"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664987"], ["No-go decay (NGD) responds to stalling during elongation at internal sense codons, typically caused by strong mRNA secondary structures, damaged bases, problematic codon runs, or specific nascent peptide sequences. Ribosomes that have little or no mRNA extending beyond the A site after cleavage are recognised by specific factors and usually induce an endonucleolytic cleavage event near the stall site, generating truncated 5′ and 3′ fragments that are then degraded 5′→3′ by Xrn1 and 3′→5′ by the exosome complex, respectively."])

openModal( this, "PKR", ["18599071","25233993"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18599071","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25233993"], ["Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is a potent danger signal recognized by the innate immune system, and protein kinase R (PKR) is one of the primary cellular sensors that mediates the antiviral response to dsRNA. A minimum dsRNA length of 30-33 bp is required to bind two PKR monomers simultaneously, which dimerize.","The presence of contaminating (dsRNA) triggers an antiviral defense network that halts global, cap-dependent translation of all proteins across the entire cell, not just the therapeutic protein encoded by the IVT mRNA. dsRNA also activates RNase L, a nonspecific endoribonuclease that degrades all cellular RNA. dsRNA can also activate RIG-1 and MDA5, triggering type I interferon production and inflammatory cytokine release."])

openModal( this, "PolyA tail", ["30503240","42212174"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30503240","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42212174"], ["The 3′ poly(A) tail of eukaryotic mRNAs plays a major role in gene expression. The Poly(A) tail serves two major functions: it protects the mRNA from 3’ degradation by deadenylases, and promotes translation by recruiting cytoplasmic poly(A)-binding proteins, which in turn promote translation by recruiting initiation factors. The downstream consequence of the progressive removal of the Poly(A) tail is the decapping.","The poly(A) length is a highly engineered component of the therapeutic mRNA. The current consensus is that the length should be around 100-150 nucleotides, which fits in the average length in endogenous eukaryotic transcripts. Moreover, poly(A) is often segmented: the tail is intercalated with a C every about 15 nucleotides. Distributing spacers along the tail has been proven to increase IVT transcription fidelity and reduce the deadenylation activity of Ccr4-Not."])

openModal( this, "PABP", ["37152278"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37152278"], ["Poly(A) binding protein (Pab1 in yeast/PABPC1 in mammals) binds the Poly(A) tail with high affinity and it interacts with translation initiation factors. Importantly, it protects mRNA from degradation: poly(A) not bound by PABP can be removed by Caf1 and Ccr4, while RNA in the binding site of PAPB can only be accessed by Ccr4. Slow translation elongation, often due to low codon optimality, results in lower levels of PAPB, engaging Caf1. Therefore, while Ccr4 is required for deadenylation of all mRNAs, Caf1 is specifically recruited when the presence of non-optimal codons result in reduced PAPB occupancy."])

openModal( this, "Translation initiation", ["32093140"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32093140"], ["In eukaryotic cells, translation initiation begins when the cap-binding complex eIF4F, which triggers recruitment of the 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC), which then scans processively along the 5′ untranslated region (5′ UTR) until it encounters the AUG start codon in the appropriate nucleotide context (the Kozak sequence), whereupon GTP hydrolysis by eIF2 commits the ribosome to initiating at that codon. Because the 5′ UTR is the very landscape through which this scanning takes place, its sequence and structure are powerful regulators of how efficiently translation is initiated: stable secondary structures such as hairpins or G-quadruplexes can stall or displace the scanning PIC, while upstream open reading frames (uORFs) can trap the ribosome before it reaches the intended AUG, both substantially reducing protein output. In therapeutic IVT-mRNA design, this mechanistic understanding is directly exploited — 5′ UTRs are engineered to minimize folding free energy, eliminate uORFs, carry a strong Kozak context, and possibly contain internal ribosomal entry sites (IRES)."])

openModal( this, "Deadenylation", ["37152278"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37152278"], ["Ccr4-Not is the primary cytoplasmic deadenylase complex and the rate-limiting initiator of mRNA decay. It contains two catalytic nuclease subunits housed in a \"deadenylase module\": (1) Caf1 (CNOT7/CNOT8 in humans): a 3'-5' exonuclease that makes base-stacking interactions with the poly(A) backbone; inhibited by PABP bound near the cleavage site. (2) Ccr4 (CNOT6/CNOT6L in humans): a phosphoesterase family enzyme that directly recognizes adenosine bases; active even when PABP is bound, and thus able to degrade the PABP-protected portion of the poly(A) tail. Ccr4-Not can be recruited by different mechanisms: by the miRNA through the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), by the presence of rare codons that make the ribosomes stall, and covalent mRNA modifications."])

openModal( this, "Decapping", ["37621215"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37621215"], ["mRNA decapping is a critical and irreversible step in mRNA turnover that removes the protective 5' m7G cap, shutting down translation and committing the mRNA to complete degradation by 5'-3' exonucleases. (1) Dpc2: a catalytic enzyme that hydrolyzes the cap structure, leaving just a 5’-monophosphate on the mRNA. (2) Dpc1: an essential coactivator hat binds Dcp2's N-terminal regulatory domain and stabilizes its catalytically active conformation. (3) Edcs: enhancer proteins that further stimulate decapping by binding both rhe mRNA substrate and the Cdp1-Dcp2 complex. It also acts as a ascafoold for assembling processing bodies (P-bodies), cytoplasmic granules where mRNA decay factors concentrate."])

openModal( this, "CAP1", ["27317694","33524237"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27317694","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33524237"], ["Cap1 (m7GpppNm) adds to CAP0 a 2'-O-methylation at the first cap-proximal nucleotide. In mammalian cells, all mature mRNAs have Cap1 structure and are recognised as \"self\", preventing activation of innate immune pathways. mRNA capping serves many functional benefits beyond immune evasion: it increases mRNA stability by protecting from exonuclease degradation, facilitates ribosome binding by recruiting initiation factions, regulates splicing and turnover.","Once therapeutic mRNA is delivered into cells via LNPs or other carriers, the amount of protein produced depends directly on how efficiently the mRNA is recognized by the eIF4F complex. eIF4E binding to the m7G cap is typically the rate-limiting step for translation initiation, making proper cap structure and eIF4F recruitment the primary determinants of protein output."])

openModal( this, "CAP0", ["27317694","24371270"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27317694", "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24371270"], ["Cap0 (m7GpppN) is the basic cap structure consisting of 7-methylguanosine (m7G) linked via a triphosphate bridge to the first nucleotide of the mRNA.","Cap0 is recognized as \"foreign\" by the innate immune system and triggers antiviral responses through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) like RIG-I, MDA5, and TLRs. Interferon-induced proteins with tetratricopeptide repeats (IFITs) specifically bind Cap0 structures and sequester them from the translation machinery, causing translational repression by various mechanisms."])

openModal( this, "CAP2", ["27317694","36725932"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27317694","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36725932"], ["Cap2 (m7GpppNmNm) includes 2'-O-methylation at both the first and second cap-proximal nucleotides. Cap2 is the result of a slow, continuous conversion from Cap1 to Cap2 as mRNAs age in the cytosol, and is therefore present on long-lived transcripts.","Cap2 provides additional protection against antiviral mechanisms: its slow accumulation ensures that levels of Cap2 are present in low amount on newly expressed viral RNAs."])

openModal( this, "Cap-binding complex", ["38880976","38287194"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38880976","https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38287194"], ["Eukaryotic translation initiation factor (eIF4F) complex consists of three core subunits that work together to initiate cap-dependent translation: (1) eIF4E: directly recognizes and binds the m7G cap structure at the end of the 5’, acting as a cap chaperone. (2) eIF4A: An ATP-dependent DEAD-box RNA helicase that unwinds secondary structures in the 5' UTR to allow ribosome scanning. (3) eIF4G: a large scaffold protein that serves as an organizing hub. It simultaneously binds eIF4E, eIF4A and PABP at the 3’ en, creating a closed loop structure that circularizes the mRNA, enhancing translation efficiency.","Once locked at the cap via eIF4E, eIF4G optimizes and localizes the helicase activity of eIF4A directly to the adjacent 5′ UTR. The ribosome is then recruited to this exact 5′ tip via the eIF4G–ribosomal interaction and begins linearly scanning downward toward the start codon (AUG)."])

openModal( this, "Translation Elongation", ["38605988"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38605988"], ["Once the ribosome has committed to an AUG and begins elongating, each codon in the open reading frame must be decoded by a cognate aminoacyl-tRNA before the next peptide bond can form; the rate of this decoding step is directly proportional to the cellular abundance of the matching tRNA. For a therapeutic mRNA, whose sequence is entirely synthetic, the codon composition may be poorly matched to the human tRNA pool, leading to slow elongation, ribosome stalling, premature termination, and ultimately lower protein yield. Codon optimization addresses this by substituting rare codons with human-preferred synonymous alternatives; however, it must be applied judiciously, because some pausing is functionally important: slowing the ribosome at domain boundaries gives the nascent polypeptide time to fold co-translationally, and uniform replacement of all non-optimal codons can therefore produce higher quantities of misfolded or aggregated protein. The current best practice thus combines global codon optimization with codon harmonization at domain junctions, guided by ribosome profiling data, to balance yield with structural fidelity of the expressed therapeutic protein."])

openModal( this, "Recycling", ["29735640"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29735640"], ["Ribosomal recycling is not merely a \"reset\" step — it is a rate-limiting determinant of overall translational output, because the total number of free ribosomal subunits available for new initiation events is set also by how rapidly post-termination complexes are disassembled. If recycling is impaired, ribosomes accumulate as stalled post-termination complexes and also \"read through\" into the 3′ UTR, triggering NMD, thereby destabilizing the very transcripts the cell is trying to express. In the context of therapeutic mRNA, ribosomal recycling has a direct practical consequence: a transcript delivered in large copy number will only sustain high protein output if ribosomes can be recycled fast enough to re-engage the same mRNA molecule repeatedly - a process further enhanced by the closed-loop architecture (PABP–eIF4G interaction)."])

openModal( this, "Translation Termination", ["9735640"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9735640"], ["eRF1 (eukaryotic release factor 1) is the class 1 release factor that directly decodes all three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) and catalyzes peptide release. After the release, eRF1 remains on the ribosome, which is critical for recruiting ABCE1. ABCE1 (ATP-binding cassette sub-family E member 1) is an essential, highly conserved twin-ATPase that splits post-termination ribosomes into their 40S and 60S subunits.When eRF1 is recruited, it induces a conformational change int he ribosome than masks the ABCE1 binding site, which in turn splits the ribosome into its two subunits. After splitting, the ribosome is recycled to enter a new translation cycle: ABCE1 remains associated witht eh 40S and interacts with initiation factors."])

openModal( this, "Pro-inflammatory cytokines", ["37834268"], ["https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37834268"], ["Driven by NF-κB rather than the IRF/IFN arm, these cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF) recruit and activate innate immune cells (monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells) at and around the injection site, producing the local inflammation and systemic reactogenicity seen after dosing. A controlled level of this is actually beneficial in vaccines, where it acts as a built-in adjuvant that matures dendritic cells and primes adaptive immunity. The problem arises when the response is excessive or prolonged. NF-κB signalling first \"primes\" the cell, raising levels of the NLRP3 sensor and of pro-IL-1β; a second signal, supplied by LNP components, ion flux, lysosomal rupture or reactive oxygen species, then triggers assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasome and activation of caspase-1. Caspase-1 does two things: it matures IL-1β and IL-18 (amplifying the inflammatory loop) and it drives pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death. The consequence for the therapeutic is direct and physical — the transfected cells that were meant to manufacture the protein are stressed or killed, which is why NLRP3 activation exerts a detrimental effect on transfection efficiency and shortens the duration of expression. This is why current formulation strategies, including m1Ψ substitution and tuning of LNP lipid composition (e.g., ionizable-lipid, cationic-lipid and cholesterol ratios that minimise NLRP3 activation), aim to keep it in check."])
